title: Origins and History
description: Basketball was invented in December 1891 by James Naismith, a physical education teacher in Springfield, Massachusetts, who needed an indoor game for winter. He nailed two peach baskets to a gym balcony, divided his class into two teams, and wrote thirteen rules: no running with the ball, no physical contact, and points scored by throwing the ball into the basket. The first baskets had bottoms, so someone had to climb up to retrieve the ball after each score, until open nets were introduced. The game spread quickly through schools, colleges, and the YMCA, became an Olympic sport in 1936, and grew into professional leagues worldwide, with the NBA the most prominent. Its appeal lies in its pace, its scoring, and its simplicity: a ball, a hoop, and ten players.

demo.code:
print('Invented:', 1891)
print('Original rules:', 13)
print('Olympic debut:', 1936)
print('Years from invention to Olympics:', 1936-1891)

Invented: 1891
Original rules: 13
Olympic debut: 1936
Years from invention to Olympics: 45

history: Basketball was invented in December 1891 in Springfield, Massachusetts, by James Naismith, who nailed peach baskets to a gym balcony.
competitions: The sport spread through schools and colleges, became Olympic in 1936, and grew into professional leagues worldwide, led by the NBA.
rules: Naismith's original thirteen rules banned running with the ball and physical contact, principles that remain in the modern game.

title: Rules and the Court
description: Basketball is played by two teams of five on a rectangular court, with a hoop 3.05 metres (10 feet) high at each end. Teams score by shooting the ball through the opponent's hoop: two points for a field goal inside the three-point arc, three points beyond it, and one point for each free throw. A player with the ball must dribble to move, and violations include travelling, carrying the ball, double dribble, and failing to shoot before the shot clock expires, 24 seconds under FIBA rules. Games are played in four quarters, 10 minutes under FIBA rules and 12 under NBA rules, with overtime if tied. Fouls are penalised with free throws or possession, and a player who commits too many fouls is disqualified.

print('Hoop height (metres):', 3.05)
print('Field goal points:', 2)
print('Three-point points:', 3)
print('Free throw points:', 1)
demo.expected_output:
Players per team on court: 5
Hoop height (metres): 3.05
Field goal points: 2
Three-point points: 3
Free throw points: 1

rules: Two teams of five play four quarters, score by shooting into a hoop 3.05 metres high, and win by scoring more points, with two points for field goals and three beyond the arc.
history: The court, hoop height, and shot clock have been standardised by federations, with FIBA and NBA rules differing in detail.
techniques: Players must dribble to move with the ball, and violations include travelling, double dribble, and shot-clock expiry.

title: Positions
description: Basketball's five traditional positions are point guard, shooting guard, small forward, power forward, and centre. The point guard runs the offence, bringing the ball up and setting up teammates; the shooting guard scores from outside and moves without the ball; the small forward is versatile, scoring and defending on the wing; the power forward plays near the basket, rebounding and scoring inside; the centre, usually the tallest player, protects the rim, rebounds, and scores close to the basket. Modern basketball is increasingly positionless, with guards posting up and centres shooting three-pointers, but the roles remain useful shorthand for what a player is asked to do. Coaches build lineups to balance scoring, defence, rebounding, and playmaking across the five spots.

positions = ['point guard', 'shooting guard', 'small forward', 'power forward', 'centre']
for i, p in enumerate(positions, 1):
    print(i, p)
print('Positions:', len(positions))
demo.expected_output:
1 point guard
2 shooting guard
3 small forward
4 power forward
5 centre
Positions: 5

techniques: Point guard, shooting guard, small forward, power forward, and centre each have distinct roles, though modern play is increasingly positionless.
training: Guards train ball-handling and passing, forwards train versatility, and centres train post play, rebounding, and rim protection.
rules: Positions are conventions, not rules: any player may shoot, pass, or defend anywhere, and coaches assign roles to suit their roster.

title: Shooting
description: Shooting is basketball's scoring skill, and it takes several forms. A jump shot, taken rising off the floor with a high release, is the standard outside shot; a layup, taken driving to the basket with one hand off the backboard, is the highest-percentage close shot; a free throw, taken unguarded from the line after a foul, rewards routine and calm; a three-pointer, taken beyond the arc, is worth an extra point and stretches defences. Good shooting shares keys across forms: balanced feet, a smooth release, a high arc, and a follow-through with the wrist snapping toward the basket. Coaches teach form first with unguarded repetition, then add movement, fatigue, and defenders, because a shot made standing still is not the same as a shot made in a game.

demo.code:
shots = 20
made = 9
print('Shots attempted:', shots)
print('Shots made:', made)
print('Field-goal percentage:', round(made / shots * 100, 1), '%')
demo.expected_output:
Shots attempted: 20
Shots made: 9
Field-goal percentage: 45.0 %

techniques: Jump shots, layups, free throws, three-pointers, and bank shots use different mechanics, with follow-through, balance, and arc as common keys.
training: Shooting practice builds form through repetition, then adds movement, fatigue, and defensive pressure to match game conditions.
statistics: Field-goal percentage, three-point percentage, and free-throw percentage measure shooting efficiency.

title: Dribbling and Ball-Handling
description: Dribbling is how a basketball player moves with the ball, bouncing it continuously with one hand while running, changing direction, and protecting it from defenders. The basics are a low, controlled dribble, a change of pace to wrong-foot a defender, and keeping the body between the ball and the opponent. Advanced moves include the crossover, switching hands in front of the body; the behind-the-back dribble; the between-the-legs dribble; and the spin move, turning past a defender. A player who stops dribbling must pass or shoot, and starting again is a double-dribble violation, so ball-handlers plan their moves to end in a pass or shot. Great ball-handling lets a player create their own shot and set up teammates, and it is practised with both hands, at speed, and under pressure.

demo.code:
dribbles = 100
lost = 4
print('Dribbles in a drill:', dribbles)
print('Balls lost:', lost)
print('Control rate:', round((dribbles - lost) / dribbles * 100, 1), '%')
demo.expected_output:
Dribbles in a drill: 100
Balls lost: 4
Control rate: 96.0 %

techniques: Crossovers, behind-the-back, between-the-legs, and spin moves beat defenders, with low dribbles, change of pace, and protection of the ball as basics.
rules: A player must dribble continuously to move with the ball; stopping and starting again is a double-dribble violation.
training: Ball-handling drills build control with both hands, at speed, and under defensive pressure.

title: Passing
description: Passing moves the ball faster than any player can dribble, and it is the foundation of team offence in basketball. The chest pass, thrown firmly from the chest with both hands, is the standard short pass; the bounce pass, bounced once before reaching a teammate, gets under a defender's hands; the overhead pass, thrown from above the head, clears tall defenders and starts fast breaks; and the no-look pass, delivered while looking elsewhere, deceives defenders. Good passing needs timing, accuracy, and anticipation: the passer must read a teammate's cut and deliver the ball where the teammate will be, not where they are. Assists, passes that lead directly to a score, are the statistic that credits playmaking, and the best passing teams create easy shots by moving the ball until the defence breaks down.

print('Passes:', passes)
print('Assists:', assists)
print('Assist rate:', round(assists / passes * 100, 1), '%')

techniques: Chest passes, bounce passes, overhead passes, and no-look passes move the ball faster than any dribble, with timing and accuracy as keys.
training: Passing drills practise accuracy on the move, passing under pressure, and reading a teammate's cut before it happens.
statistics: Assists, passes leading directly to a score, measure a player's playmaking contribution.

title: Defense
description: Defence in basketball is a five-player job, built on stance, footwork, and communication. In man-to-man defence, each defender guards one opponent, staying between them and the basket, sliding laterally, and contesting shots without fouling. In zone defence, defenders guard areas, shifting together as the ball moves, which protects the basket but can concede outside shots. Teams also press, defending full-court to force turnovers, and switch assignments on screens to avoid mismatches. Help defence is the key concept: when a teammate is beaten, another defender steps in, and the team rotates to cover the open player. Fouls limit defence, since illegal contact gives free throws or possession, and a defender who fouls out leaves the team short.

techniques: Man-to-man defence, zone defence, pressing, and switching cover different threats, with stance, footwork, and communication as basics.
rules: Defenders may not hold, push, or impede illegally; fouls give the offence free throws or possession depending on the rules and foul count.
training: Defensive drills practise slides, closeouts, help defence, and rotations, since defence is a five-player responsibility.

title: Rebounding
description: Rebounding is winning the ball after a missed shot, and it often decides close games. A defensive rebound ends the opponent's possession and starts a team's own attack, while an offensive rebound gives a second scoring chance, sometimes with a putback score at the rim. The fundamentals are boxing out, using the body to block an opponent from the basket, timing the jump to meet the ball at its highest point, and securing it with two hands before landing. Rebounding rewards positioning and effort more than height alone: a shorter player who boxes out well and jumps at the right time will out-rebound a taller player who watches the ball. Coaches track rebounds per player and per team, and they value offensive rebounds highly, because an extra possession is an extra chance to score.

techniques: Boxing out, timing the jump, and securing the ball with two hands are rebounding fundamentals, with offensive and defensive rebounds as distinct skills.
training: Rebounding drills practise positioning, contact, and second efforts, since rebounds often decide close games.
statistics: Rebounds are counted per player and team, with offensive rebounds giving extra scoring chances.

title: Fast Break
description: The fast break is basketball's quickest offence: after a rebound, steal, or made basket, the team with the ball sprints up the court before the defence can set up, aiming for an easy layup or open shot. It starts with an outlet pass from the rebounder to a guard, who pushes the ball up the middle while teammates fill the lanes on either side, running wide and ahead of the ball. The ball handler reads the defence: if a defender commits, they pass to the open teammate; if the lane is clear, they drive to the basket. Fast breaks last only seconds, so decision-making at speed is the skill, and teams that rebound well and pass quickly create the most break chances. A good break turns defence into offence in one motion, and it energises a team and a crowd.

techniques: Fast breaks start with a rebound or steal, an outlet pass, and lanes filled by sprinting teammates, finishing with a layup or open shot.
training: Break drills practise outlet passing, lane discipline, and decision-making at speed, since a break lasts only seconds.
rules: No special rules govern fast breaks; the same travelling, foul, and out-of-bounds rules apply at full speed.

title: Half-Court Offense
description: Half-court offence is what a team does when the defence is already set, and it is where most basketball games are won. The pick-and-roll is its central play: a teammate sets a screen for the ball handler, who uses it to drive, shoot, or pass to the screener rolling to the basket. Off-ball screens free shooters, spacing keeps defenders spread out so they cannot help on drives, and ball movement, passing until the defence shifts out of position, creates open shots. Patience matters: a good half-court team may pass several times before shooting, waiting for a high-percentage chance rather than forcing a contested one. Late in the shot clock, teams need a reliable play and a player who can create a shot under pressure.

techniques: Pick-and-roll, off-ball screens, spacing, and ball movement create shots against a set defence, with patience and execution as keys.
training: Half-court drills practise set plays, reads against different defences, and late-clock execution.
statistics: Points per possession in the half court measure how efficiently a team scores when it cannot run.

title: Training and Conditioning
description: Basketball training prepares players for a game of sprints, jumps, lateral movement, and skill under fatigue. A typical week mixes skill sessions for shooting, passing, and ball-handling, team practices for offence and defence, strength and conditioning for power and injury prevention, and recovery after games. Coaches plan load across the season, building fitness early and maintaining it during competition, because overtraining causes injuries and under-training leaves players unable to sustain intensity. Jumping and landing technique is a focus, since knees and ankles take heavy loads in basketball, and prevention exercises are standard. Conditioning is position-specific in detail: guards need repeated sprint ability, forwards need versatility, and centres need strength and rebounding endurance.

training: Basketball training mixes skill work, scrimmages, strength and conditioning, and recovery, with load planned across a season.
safety: Warm-ups, ankle and knee prevention, and load management reduce injuries, with jumping and landing technique a focus.
techniques: Conditioning demands include repeated sprints, lateral movement, jumping, and endurance, with position-specific programmes.

title: Refereeing
description: Refereeing in basketball is the work of calling fouls and violations fairly while play moves at high speed. Crews of two or three officials rotate positions to cover the court, calling travelling, double dribble, and shot-clock violations, personal fouls for illegal contact, and technical fouls for misconduct. Table officials track the score, fouls, time, and shot clock, and video review assists in major competitions for decisions such as whether a shot beat the buzzer or was a two- or three-pointer. Referees train for fitness, positioning, clear signals, and communication with players and coaches, and they are assessed after games. Their decisions are final on the court, and respect for officials is part of basketball's culture.

techniques: Officials train in positioning, signals, communication, and fitness, and rotate positions to cover the whole court.
history: Officiating has grown with the game, with two- and three-person crews standard at higher levels and video review in major competitions.

title: Major Leagues and Competitions
description: Basketball's major competitions span leagues and tournaments. The NBA, founded in 1946, is the world's premier professional league, with a regular season followed by playoffs in best-of-seven series that crown a champion. The WNBA, founded in 1996, is the leading women's professional league. In Europe, the EuroLeague gathers top clubs, and domestic leagues run in every basketball country. Internationally, FIBA runs the World Cup, begun in 1950, and Olympic basketball, played since 1936, where national teams compete for gold. The formats differ, leagues reward consistency across a season, tournaments reward nerve in knockout rounds, but the game at the top is the same fast, high-scoring contest invented in Springfield.

print('Olympic basketball since:', 1936)

competitions: The NBA, WNBA, EuroLeague, and FIBA World Cup and Olympic tournaments are basketball's premier competitions.
history: The NBA was founded in 1946, the WNBA in 1996, and the FIBA World Cup began in 1950, with Olympic basketball since 1936.
rules: Leagues use regular seasons followed by playoffs, with series deciding champions, while tournaments use group stages and knockouts.

title: Women's Basketball
description: Women's basketball began almost as soon as the men's game, with the first women's college game played in 1893, only two years after Naismith's invention, and it has grown into a major sport in its own right. Women's Olympic basketball began in 1976, the WNBA was founded in 1996 as a professional league, and the FIBA Women's World Cup crowns world champions. The women's game follows the same rules and uses the same court, with a slightly smaller ball in most competitions, and it features the same skills, tactics, and athleticism as the men's game. Audiences and participation have grown sharply in recent years, and closing remaining gaps in pay, facilities, and coverage is a central task for the sport.

history: Women's basketball began soon after the men's game, with the first women's college game in 1893, and grew into professional leagues and Olympic competition.
competitions: The WNBA, Olympic women's basketball, and the FIBA Women's World Cup are the premier women's competitions.
statistics: Audiences and participation for women's basketball have grown sharply, though pay and coverage gaps remain in many leagues.

title: 3x3 Basketball
description: 3x3 basketball is basketball's half-court, three-a-side form, played on one basket with two teams of three and a substitute each. The first team to 21 points wins, or the team leading after 10 minutes, with a 12-second shot clock keeping play fast. Possession alternates after scores in some rules, and the game is played outdoors and indoors, often to music, in tournaments that feel like festivals. 3x3 grew from streetball and pickup games into a FIBA-governed sport, with a World Cup and an Olympic debut at Tokyo 2020. It rewards one-on-one skill, quick decisions, and outside shooting, and it is an accessible entry point to basketball, needing only a half court, one hoop, and six players.

rules: Two teams of three play on a half court to 21 points or a 10-minute limit, with one basket, a 12-second shot clock, and first possession decided by a coin toss.
history: 3x3 grew from streetball and pickup games into a FIBA-governed sport and an Olympic event, debuting at Tokyo 2020.
techniques: Quick decisions, one-on-one skill, and outside shooting matter most, with no coaches on the sideline during play in many events.

title: Wheelchair Basketball
description: Wheelchair basketball is basketball played in sports wheelchairs, with two teams of five on a standard court and a hoop at standard height. Players push their chairs, dribble, pass, and shoot, following basketball rules adapted for chairs, including rules about travelling with the ball and contact between chairs. Athletes are classified by functional ability on a points scale, and the total classification points of the five players on court may not exceed a set limit, so teams balance players of different classifications. The sport grew from rehabilitation after the Second World War into a major Paralympic sport, with professional and club leagues worldwide. It demands upper-body strength, chair skill, and all the passing, shooting, and tactical skill of the running game.
